name: curl
description: A command-line tool for transferring data to or from servers using HTTP, HTTPS, FTP and many other protocols.

flags.description: -O: write output to a file / save with the remote filename.
Fetch only the HTTP headers (HEAD request).
Set the HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE).
Send POST data; -d '{"k":1}' -H "Content-Type: application/json" for JSON APIs.

examples.explanation: Prints the response body to the terminal.
Downloads the file, keeping its remote filename.
Follows redirects and saves the final page to page.html.
Checks status code and headers without downloading the body — the fastest health check for a URL.
Sends a JSON POST request to an API — the standard quick API test.
Uploads a file as multipart/form-data, like an HTML form.

about: curl speaks many protocols and gives fine control over requests: headers, methods, auth, cookies, proxies, timeouts, and TLS options. It writes response bodies to stdout by default, which makes it composable in scripts. For interactive downloads with resume, wget is often more convenient; for detailed API work, curl -v shows the full request/response exchange.
useCases: Check service health with curl -I or curl -fsS.
mistakes: Forgetting -L and getting a 301 redirect page instead of content.
Posting JSON without the Content-Type header.
Using -k in production and silently accepting invalid certificates.
warnings: curl prints secrets (tokens in headers/URLs) to your shell history and terminal; avoid pasting credentials in commands, use config files or environment variables.
distroNotes: curl is preinstalled on nearly every distribution and macOS. Windows 10+ includes it too.
